sections.h: Warnings by the Spirit on the road to Jerusalem
sections.b: On Paul's last journey to Jerusalem the Spirit speaks again and again through believers. At Tyre the disciples tell Paul "through the Spirit" not to set foot in Jerusalem (Acts 21:4); at Caesarea the prophet Agabus says, "The Holy Spirit says this," and acts out Paul's binding (Acts 21:11). Paul had already said he was going "bound in the Spirit," warned in every city that chains awaited him (Acts 20:22–23). Most readers take the Spirit to reveal the suffering, and the believers' pleas to come from love; a minority think Paul went against the Spirit's warning. Luke's frame is that Paul's going is the Lord's will (Acts 21:14; 23:11).

uncommon: Some readers think Paul disobeyed the Spirit by going up to Jerusalem, and that his arrest followed from it.

sections.b: Acts 21 gathers prophets in one house at Caesarea: Philip's four unmarried daughters, who prophesied (Acts 21:9), and Agabus from Judea, who had foretold the famine under Claudius (Acts 11:28). Agabus acts out his message like Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, binding his own hands and feet with Paul's belt, and introduces it with a messenger formula, "The Holy Spirit says this" (Acts 21:11). In the event, Roman soldiers put Paul in chains after Jews from Asia seized him (Acts 21:30–33). Readers debate whether this shows New Testament prophecy could be true in substance but loose in detail (Wayne Grudem) or simply a summary that Paul himself later repeats (Acts 28:17).

common: Agabus' prophecy came true: Paul was handed over to the Romans because of the Jews' accusations.
uncommon: New Testament prophecy, unlike the Old Testament prophets' words, could be inspired yet mistaken in detail.

sections.b: At Caesarea Paul stays with Philip the evangelist, who "had four daughters, virgins who prophesied" (Acts 21:9), fulfilling Joel's promise quoted at Pentecost that sons and daughters would prophesy (Acts 2:17). Luke gives none of them a word to say; the next prophecy comes from Agabus. Later Christians remembered them: Papias heard stories from them, and Polycrates of Ephesus said they were buried at Hierapolis and Ephesus (Eusebius, Church History 3.31; 3.39). The verse is cited on every side of the debate over women's ministry; the Where Christians differ card at Acts 21 asks whether prophesying is the same as preaching or church office.

sections.h: James receives Paul for the last time
sections.b: When Paul reaches Jerusalem around AD 57, he reports to James and all the elders (Acts 21:18–19). James praises God for the Gentiles, but warns that tens of thousands of Jewish believers, "all of them zealous for the law," have heard Paul teaches Jews to abandon Moses, and proposes that Paul sponsor four men's vow in the temple (Acts 21:20–24). The scene shows James as the leader of a law-observant Jewish church who still affirms the decree freeing Gentiles from circumcision (Acts 21:25). It is his last appearance in Acts; Josephus says he was stoned in AD 62 (Antiquities 20.200).

sections.h: Did Paul teach Jews to abandon Moses?
sections.b: In Acts 21 the Jerusalem elders say the believing Jews of Judea are "zealous for the law" and have been told that Paul teaches Jews living among Gentiles "to desert Moses," not to circumcise their children or keep the customs (Acts 21:20–21). Luke calls the rumor false, and Paul proves his observance by joining a temple purification (Acts 21:24–26). Readers differ: the "Paul within Judaism" view holds that Paul never told Jews to stop keeping the law; many Protestant readers think his teaching loosened Jewish observance in practice; critical scholars since Vielhauer suspect Acts makes Paul more law-observant than his letters do (compare 1 Corinthians 7:18; 9:20; Galatians 5:2).

uncommon: Paul remained a fully law-observant Jew all his life and taught Jewish believers to do the same.

sections.h: The rumor that Paul opposed circumcision for Jews
sections.b: Jewish believers in Jerusalem had heard that Paul told Jews abroad "not to circumcise their children" (Acts 21:21). Acts presents this as false: Paul circumcised Timothy, whose mother was Jewish (Acts 16:3), and in his letters he told the circumcised not to undo it (1 Corinthians 7:18), while insisting Gentiles must not be circumcised (Galatians 5:2). The elders restate that Gentile believers are bound only by the four requirements of the decree (Acts 21:25).

To answer the rumor that he despised the law, Paul agreed to go through purification with four Jewish believers who had "taken a vow on themselves" and to pay for the offerings that ended it, when they would shave their heads (Acts 21:23–26; Numbers 6:13–20). Paying a poor Nazirite's costs was a known act of piety (Josephus, Antiquities 19.294). In Acts 23 another kind of vow appears: more than forty men put themselves under a curse not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul (Acts 23:12–14, 21). The Mishnah lists vows that could be released when circumstances made them impossible (Mishnah Nedarim 3:1, 3).

sections.h: Paul in the temple and the warning stone
sections.b: Paul's arrest happens in the temple. He was there completing a purification with four Nazirites when Jews from Asia accused him of bringing Greeks inside and making "this holy place common" (Acts 21:26–28). Inscribed stones along the barrier between the outer and inner courts threatened death to any foreigner who passed it; one complete stone (found 1871) and a fragment (1935) survive, and Josephus describes them (Jewish War 5.193–194). The gates were shut behind Paul (Acts 21:30), and no believer enters the temple again in Acts. In his speech Paul says his mission to the Gentiles came to him in a vision while he prayed in the temple (Acts 22:17–21).

claude.title: Claude's theory: "common" as a frame
claude.body: The charge that Paul made the temple "common" (Acts 21:28) uses the same word as Peter's vision, "What God has made clean, you must not call common" (Acts 10:15). I suggest Luke lets the shared word frame the second half of Acts: who decides what is common, the temple barrier or the God who cleansed Gentile hearts by faith (Acts 15:9)?

sections.b: Paul, back from years in Gentile lands, undergoes a seven-day purification before the offerings for four Nazirites (Acts 21:24–27), probably the cleansing from corpse impurity in Numbers 19:11–12. His accusers say he made the holy place "common" by bringing in a Gentile (Acts 21:28), using the word that Peter's vision forbade believers to use of what God had cleansed (Acts 10:15).

James and the elders remind Paul that for Gentile believers the Jerusalem church ruled only that they keep away from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled and from sexual sin (Acts 21:25; compare Acts 15:20, 29). Most readers take the reminder as assurance that nothing new is being asked of Gentiles; some critical scholars think Paul's letters show no knowledge of the decree (1 Corinthians 8–10; Galatians 2:6).

sections.h: Paul, a Roman citizen in Roman custody
sections.b: Roman soldiers rescue Paul from the temple mob (Acts 21:31–36). About to be flogged for questioning, he asks whether it is lawful to whip a Roman citizen uncondemned, and the interrogation stops (Acts 22:24–29); the old laws protected citizens, and Cicero's speech against Verres shows the outrage at breaking them. The commander, Claudius Lysias, had bought his citizenship, as Cassius Dio says people did under Claudius; Paul was born a citizen (Acts 22:28). Lysias sends Paul under heavy guard to the governor Felix with a letter finding no crime (Acts 23:23–30). Many scholars see in these chapters Luke's interest in showing Rome that Christianity was no threat; others stress Rome's corruption in the next chapters.

By the late 50s there were disciples in Tyre. Paul's ship unloaded there for a week, and the believers warned Paul through the Spirit not to go to Jerusalem; then whole families, wives and children, walked him to the beach and knelt to pray (Acts 21:3–6). The city that the prophets had condemned for its pride (Ezekiel 26–28) and that Jesus said would have repented at his miracles (Matthew 11:21–22) now had a church.

Paul's last visit to Jerusalem (Acts 21:15–23:30) begins with a warm welcome from the church and ends with a riot in the temple, a near lynching in the Sanhedrin, a sworn plot to kill him, and a night escape under 470 soldiers. From here the story moves away from Jerusalem for good, toward Rome (Acts 23:11).

Paul tells the Jerusalem crowd he studied at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), and tells the Sanhedrin, in the present tense, "I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees," on trial for the hope of the resurrection (Acts 23:6). Some Pharisee scribes then defend him: "We find nothing bad about this man" (Acts 23:9). In Acts the Pharisees are often moderate or friendly (Acts 5:34–39; 15:5), and the hostile group is the priestly leadership. Readers debate whether Paul's cry was a tactic or the honest center of his case.
sections.refs: Acts 5:34–39; Acts 15:5; Acts 22:3; Acts 23:6–9; Acts 26:5; Philippians 3:5

sections.b: Before the Sanhedrin Paul says he is being judged "because of hope and the resurrection of the dead" (Acts 23:6), which splits the council between Pharisees, who believed in the resurrection, and Sadducees, who denied it (Acts 23:7–8). He returns to the same hope in every later defense (Acts 24:15, 21; 26:6–8; 28:20): Jesus' resurrection is the first fruit of the resurrection Israel hoped for.

Acts 23:8 says the Sadducees deny "resurrection, angel and spirit," while the Pharisees affirm "both." Since the Sadducees accepted the books of Moses, which mention angels, readers ask what they denied. Views: they rejected the developed angelology of their time; or, as David Daube argued, "angel" and "spirit" are forms in which the dead were thought to exist before the resurrection (compare Acts 12:15, "It is his angel"), so the Sadducees denied any life after death. The Pharisee scribes then suggest that "a spirit spoke to him, or an angel" (Acts 23:9).

In his speech on the temple stairs Paul confesses that when "they were spilling the blood of Stephen, your witness," he stood by approving and guarding the cloaks of the killers (Acts 22:20). The Greek martys, "witness," is here joined to blood, a step toward its later meaning "martyr." The charge against Paul in the temple echoes the charge against Stephen (Acts 6:13; 21:28).
sections.refs: Acts 6:13; Acts 7:58–8:1; Acts 21:28; Acts 22:20; Revelation 2:13; Revelation 17:6

sections.b: In Paul's own telling of his conversion, Ananias says, "Stand up and have yourself baptized, and have your sins washed away as you call on his name" (Acts 22:16). Both verbs are in the Greek middle voice. Sacramental churches read the verse as baptism truly washing away sin; Reformed churches as baptism sealing a washing received by faith; Baptists as a believer's act picturing a cleansing already received. The Where Christians differ card at Acts 22 sets out the views.

In these chapters "the Jews" usually means a particular group: Jews from Asia who accused Paul (Acts 21:27), the leaders who brought charges (Acts 22:30), or the forty who swore to kill him (Acts 23:12). The same chapters show tens of thousands of law-keeping Jewish believers (Acts 21:20), Pharisee scribes who defend Paul (Acts 23:9) and Paul's own nephew (Acts 23:16). The Byzantine text reads "some of the Jews" at Acts 23:12, which looks like a copyist's softening. Reading these verses as a verdict on the Jewish people misreads them.

The high priest who ordered Paul struck (Acts 23:2) held office about AD 47–59. Josephus describes his wealth and violence: his servants seized the tithes due to poorer priests (Antiquities 20.205–207), and rebels killed him in AD 66 (Jewish War 2.441–442). Paul called him a "wall painted with whitewash," then apologized, quoting Exodus 22:28 (Acts 23:3–5).

Felix kept Paul "in Herod's Praetorium" (Acts 23:35), the seaside palace Herod the Great built at Caesarea, which had become the residence of Rome's governors. Its remains have been excavated on a point of land south of the harbor.

The Jerusalem crowd listened to Paul until he said the Lord had told him, "I am going to send you out to the Gentiles, far away" (Acts 22:21). Coming after the charge that he had brought Greeks into the temple (Acts 21:28), the words sounded to them like proof. Paul saw his Gentile mission as serving Israel (Romans 11:13–14) and as fulfilling Isaiah's promise of peace to those far and near (Isaiah 57:19; Acts 2:39).

The day after the riot, the Roman commander calls the chief priests and "all the Sanhedrin" together to learn the charge against Paul (Acts 22:30). The hearing collapses: the high priest has Paul struck, Paul declares himself a Pharisee on trial for the resurrection, and the Pharisees and Sadducees fall to fighting (Acts 23:1–10). Historians debate whether a tribune could summon the council; Sherwin-White judged it plausible as an informal hearing. The chief priests and elders are then approached by forty men sworn to kill Paul (Acts 23:14–15).

Luke explains that "Sadducees claim there is no resurrection, no angel, and no spirit" (Acts 23:8), which is why Paul's cry about the resurrection split the council. The high priest Ananias and the chief priests who received the plotters (Acts 23:14) belonged to the Sadducean circle (compare Acts 5:17).

Paul says he could not see because of "the glory of that light" on the road to Damascus (Acts 22:11), the word for God's visible glory. His letters describe the same moment as God shining in the heart to give the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

sections.h: "Jesus the Nazarene" on the Damascus road
sections.b: Only in Paul's speech to the Jerusalem crowd does the voice say, "I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting" (Acts 22:8), the name by which the city knew him (John 19:19). Later Christians would be called "the sect of the Nazarenes" (Acts 24:5).
